title: Secure and Insecure Attachment
objective: After this level you can explain Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation and the attachment styles it describes.
summary: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation watches how toddlers react when a caregiver leaves and returns. It sorts attachment into secure, avoidant and resistant types, with disorganized added later.

cards.headline: A stranger walks in. The parent walks out. Watch the baby.
cards.body: Harlow showed that comfort builds a bond. But do all children bond the same way? In 1970, Mary Ainsworth published a short, carefully staged scene designed to find out. The telling moments are the goodbye, and the hello that follows.

cards.headline: The Strange Situation
cards.body: Ainsworth built on John Bowlby's idea of a secure base: a caregiver whose presence lets a child feel safe enough to explore. In her Strange Situation, a caregiver and a young child spend time in a room with toys. A stranger comes in, the caregiver leaves the child with the stranger, then returns a few minutes later. Ainsworth sorted children by how they responded to the separation and to the reunion.

cards.headline: Three ways to meet a returning parent

items.label: Secure
points: Uses the caregiver as a secure base
Upset at the goodbye, happy at the return

items.label: Avoidant
points: Doesn't seem to mind the caregiver leaving
Reacts to the caregiver much as to a stranger

items.label: Resistant
points: Clingy and too fearful to explore
Very upset at separation, hard to comfort on return

cards.headline: A snapshot, not a verdict
cards.body: Ainsworth named three types; Mary Main and Judith Solomon described a fourth, disorganized, in 1990. The scheme has critics too. A child's temperament may strongly shape how they react, and attachment varies across cultures in ways the original research didn't account for. Comparing the United States and Japan, Fred Rothbaum and colleagues argued in 2000 that the measures lean on Western values like autonomy and exploration. A style describes behavior in one staged scene, not the worth of a child or a family.

cards.headline: Secure and insecure attachment
learned: The Strange Situation stages a goodbye and a reunion
Secure is the most common type; avoidant and resistant are insecure
Temperament and culture shape the picture

questions.prompt: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, the most common attachment type is _____.

options.label: avoidant
options.rationale: Avoidant children seem not to mind the caregiver leaving; it isn't the most common type.

options.label: resistant
options.rationale: Resistant children are clingy and hard to comfort; it isn't the most common type.

options.label: disorganized
options.rationale: Disorganized was added later as a fourth type.

questions.explanation: Secure attachment is the most common type: the child uses the caregiver as a secure base.

questions.prompt: Match each attachment type with how the child acts.

pairs.right: Doesn't seem to mind the caregiver

questions.explanation: A secure child is upset at the goodbye and happy at the return. An avoidant child doesn't seem to mind the caregiver leaving. A resistant child is very upset at separation and hard to comfort on return.

questions.prompt: Level 8 said naturalistic observation can't make behavior happen on schedule. How does the Strange Situation get around that?

options.label: It watches families at home without being noticed
options.rationale: That is naturalistic observation itself, with the same limit.

options.label: It stages the separation and the reunion in a room
It asks parents to fill in a long survey
options.rationale: Surveys rely on self-reports, not staged behavior.

options.label: It studies one unusual child in great depth

questions.explanation: Instead of waiting for a goodbye to happen, the Strange Situation stages one: the caregiver leaves and returns on cue.
